ca_buttermilks_main.blurb: Buttermilks Main is a hillside of large granite boulders in the Buttermilk Country of the Eastern Sierra, near Bishop, at roughly 6,400 feet. It is almost purely bouldering, and the grade spread is wide: a good base of easy and moderate problems in the low V grades, a deep middle range, and a thinner tail of hard lines into the double digits. The granite has an abrasive grain that wears skin quickly, and some of the boulders are tall enough to be real highballs. Landings at the base tend to be flat and sandy. Peabody Boulders, the Cave Area and the Stained Glass/Flyboy Area are among its largest groupings.

nv_mount_potosi.blurb: Mount Potosi is a limestone mountain about an hour west of Las Vegas and one of the main sport climbing hubs for the city. Nearly everything is bolted. Most routes sit between 5.10 and 5.12, with a modest number of easier lines in the 5.6 to 5.9 range and a harder tail reaching 5.14. Rock quality varies from crag to crag, though most of the established climbing is on good stone. The climbing is split across the West Side, North Side and East Side. Sunnier crags, such as the steep, gymnastic cave on the east side, stay comfortable through much of winter, while shadier crags higher up suit all but the hottest summer days.

wa_far_side.blurb: Far Side is a cluster of mostly bolted crags on the north side of I-90, east of Seattle near North Bend and Exit 38. Sport routes lead, with a large bouldering contingent and only a few trad lines. Grades run from beginner terrain up to 5.12, centered on 5.7 to 5.11, and the boulder problems are mostly in the lower V grades. The rock changes a lot over short distances, from frictiony and granite-like faces to bullet-hard and chossier walls, and most crags face south. Interstate Park is the largest of its subareas, alongside Overhaul, Gun Show and the Pistol Boulders.

nv_pine_creek_canyon.blurb: Pine Creek Canyon is a side canyon of Red Rocks in southern Nevada, a desert setting with pines and a stream that runs in places all year. Trad climbing dominates, on sandstone, with a smaller set of boulders. Grades spread widely, with the most climbs between 5.7 and 5.10, plenty of easier routes below that, and a thinner top end into the low 5.13s. Mescalito is the biggest sub-area and holds some very long multi-pitch routes, with the summit taking ten to twelve pitches. Brass Wall, Stick Gully and Magic Mountain follow in size. The sandstone is fragile when wet.

nm_foothills_bouldering.blurb: Foothills Bouldering covers the boulders along the western foot of the Sandia Mountains on the east side of Albuquerque, at around 6,200 feet. The boulders are coarse-grained granite, and the problems are technical. Nearly all of it is bouldering, with a broad spread: lots of easy and moderate problems, a solid middle in V3 to V5, and a harder tail up into the double digits. The area is spread over many small clusters rather than one big field. U-Mound is the busiest, joined by Fat City and Indian School, Three Gun and the Manitoba/Montgomery Trailhead. Climbing is possible all year, and warm sunny winter days suit the foothills boulders well.

ny_k_northern_region.blurb: The Northern Region covers the northern stretch of the Adirondacks, around Saranac Lake. Bouldering and trad share the load, with a smaller amount of sport and some ice. Most roped climbs fall at 5.9 to 5.10, with easier ones and a short run of 5.11 and 5.12 above that, and the boulder problems are mostly in the low and middle V grades. McKenzie Pond has four boulder zones of clean granite with over 200 problems, reached by short, well-defined trails with little elevation gain. Silver Lake offers 14 or more cliffs on two mountains, with spring and fall the best times, and more insects than most Adirondack areas. Azure Mountain adds rock, ice and mixed climbing.
